## Title
Kisan Credit Card

## Agricultural Domain
Schemes

## Scope
Central

## Scheme ID
kcc

## Scheme Introduction
KCC-Modified Interest Subvention Scheme (MISS) provides interest subvention of 1.5% per annum on short term loans for Agriculture and allied activities through Kisan Credit Card (KCC) upto Rs. 3.00 lakhs to the lending Institutions and 3% on account of Prompt Re-payment Incentive (PRI) to farmers who have made timely payments. Benefit of IS and PRI on short term loan (i.e. crop loan + allied activities including Animal Husbandry, Dairy, Fisheries, Bee Keeping etc.) through KCС are available on an overall limit of Rs. 3 lakh per annum and subject to a maximum sublimit of Rs. 2 lakh per farmer involved in allied activities related to Animal Husbandry, Dairy, Fisheries, Bee Keeping etc. within the prescribed limit of Rs. 3.00 lakh for MISS The Kisan Credit Card scheme aims at providing adequate and timely credit support from the banking system under a single window with the flexible and simplified procedures to the farmers for their cultivation and other needs as indicated below : a) To meet the short term credit requirements for the cultivation of crops; b) Post-harvest expenses; c) Produce marketing loan; d) Consumption requirements of farmer household; e) Working capital for maintenance of farm assets and activities allied to agriculture; f) Investment credit requirement for agriculture and allied activities KCC is a card provided to farmers to get easy access to credit for agriculture and allied activities. A smart Kisan Credit Card is an electronic debit card that allows farmers to withdraw money from ATMs, PoS machines, and perform mobile-based transactions. KCC provides both short-term credit for crops and long-term loans for investments like farm equipment or land development. KCC limit increases by 10% each year to account for cost escalation and inflation, subject to the bank’s review. Apart from optional crop insurance, you can opt for asset insurance, health insurance, and accident insurance through your KCC account.

## Scheme Benefits
Under the KCC - MISS scheme, farmers receive the following benefits: 1. Interest Subvention (IS): Farmers receive loans at a subvented interest rate of 7% per annum (up to ₹3 lakh for crops; up to ₹2 lakh for allied activities). 2. Prompt Repayment Incentive (PRI): An additional 3% interest incentive is given for prompt and timely repayment, reducing the effective interest rate to 4% per annum. 3. Relief to farmers affected by natural calamities, the applicable rate of interest subvention for that year will be made available to banks for the first year on the restructured loan amount. Such restructured loans will attract normal rate of interest from the second year onwards as per extant policy laid down by the RBI. 4. Relief to the farmers affected due to severe natural calamities, the applicable rate of interest subvention for that year will be made available to banks for first three years/ entire period (subject to a maximum of five years) on the restructured loan amount. Further, in all such cases, the benefit of prompt repayment incentive @3% per annum shall also be provided to the affected farmers. 5. In order to discourage distress sale by farmers and to encourage them instead to store their produce in warehouse, the benefit of interest subvention will be available to small and marginal farmers having Kisan Credit Card for a further period upto six months of postharvest of the crop on the produce stored in warehouse accredited with Warehousing Development Regulatory Authority (WDRA) against negotiable warehouse receipts, at the same rate as is available on agri loan through KCC. 6. Enhanced the collateral free loans form ₹ 1.6 lakhs to ₹ 2 lakhs per farmer under KCC scheme from 1st January 2025.

## Scheme Eligibility
Following people are eligible for KCC: a) Any individual farmer who is an owner-cultivator. b) People who belong to a group and are joint borrowers. The group has to be owner- cultivators. c) Sharecroppers, tenant farmers, or an oral lessee are eligible for the KCC. Self-help groups (SHG) or joint liability groups (JLG) of sharecroppers, farmers, tenant farmers, etc. You will need basic identification and land ownership/lease documents. In the first year, a more detailed documentation is required. KCC is typically valid for 5 years, subject to review and enhancement based on cropping patterns and needs. Farmers, including individual owner-cultivators, tenant farmers, sharecroppers, and groups like SHGs and JLGs, are eligible. you can get a term loan under KCC for allied agricultural activities like dairy, poultry, and farm equipment purchase. Marginal farmers can get a flexible limit of ₹10,000 to ₹50,000 depending on their land holding and crops grown. The credit limit can be adjusted based on the number and type of crops grown each year. There is no minimum land requirement.

## Scheme Support
Farmers can approach local bank officials, district-level nodal officers, or agriculture department representatives for grievance redressal. Banks and lending institutions will use their current systems of grievance redressal mechanism. Grievances raised by banks (in reference to the loan/claim applications) are dealt directly by DAFW, Ministry of Agriculture. For Kisan Rin Portal, the grievance redressal mechanism is in the development process.

## Additional Information
KCC is typically valid for 5 years, subject to review and enhancement based on cropping patterns and needs. The repayment is usually linked to the harvest and marketing of crops. Term loans may have specific repayment schedules based on the investment. Yes, your KCC can be renewed, and your credit limit may be revised based on your needs and cropping pattern. If a farmer can't repay my loan due to a natural calamity, banks may extend or reschedule their repayment period to accommodate the circumstances. Banks may charge processing and inspection fees, but it varies from bank to bank. Loans up to ₹1 lakh generally don’t require collateral. For loans up to ₹3 lakh with recovery tie-ups, collateral may also be waived. The loan is based on the scale of finance for your crop, area cultivated, and additional costs like maintenance and insurance. Under Interest Subvention scheme, the government offers interest rate relief on short-term crop loans, encouraging timely repayment. If you default, your account may be classified as a non-performing asset (NPA), which could impact your future loan eligibility. If you change your cropping pattern, your bank can revise your credit limit based on the new crop's scale of finance and the area cultivated. You can apply for a term loan component under KCC to purchase farm equipment, which is repayable over a longer period. If input costs rise beyond the 10% yearly increase, you can request a revision of your KCC limit from your bank. Delayed repayments may attract penalties, and the account could be classified as a non- performing asset (NPA) if not repaid within the stipulated time. You can request a revision of your credit limit during the year, and if needed, banks can enhance your limit based on input cost escalations.

## Scheme Application
Following are the application methods: Farmers can approach their nearest bank branch (of Public Sector Banks, RRBs, Cooperative Banks, or Private Sector Scheduled Commercial Banks) with the required documents for KCC application. You will need basic identification and land ownership/lease documents. In the first year, a more detailed documentation is required.

## Title
PRADHAN MANTRI KISAN SAMMAN NIDHI SCHEME (PM-KISAN SCHEME)  OPERATIONAL GUIDELINES  

## Agricultural Domain
Schemes

## Scheme ID

## Scheme Introduction
Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) is a Central Sector Scheme to provide income support to all cultivable landholding farmers' families in the country to supplement their financial needs for procuring various inputs related to agriculture and allied activities as well as to fulfil domestic needs.

Under the PM-KISAN scheme, all landholding farmers' families shall be provided the financial benefit of Rs.6,000 per annum per family payable in three equal instalments of Rs.2,000 each, every four months/trimester, i.e. April-July, August-November and December-March.



## Scheme Benefits
The scheme aims to supplement the financial needs of all landholding farmers' families in procuring various inputs to ensure proper crop health and appropriate yields, commensurate with the anticipated farm income as well as for domestic needs. Under the Scheme an amount of Rs.6,000/- per year is released by the Central Government online directly into the beneficiaries Aadhaar seeded bank accounts of the eligible farmers through Direct Benefit Transfer mode,  subject to certain exclusions.

The PM-KISAN scheme is an entitlement-based scheme subject to certain exclusion criteria.

Beneficiaries under the scheme are identified and  verified by the respective State and Union Territory  as per the operational guidelines of the scheme. The details of farmers are being maintained by the States/UTs. To make integrated platform available in the country to assist in benefit transfer, a platform named PM-KISAN Portal available at URL        (https://pmkisan.gov.in) has been launched for uploading the farmers details at a single web-portal in a uniform structure along with a dedicated PM-KISAN mobile application to address the Farmers concerns, queries and aid them in completing the mandatory requirements.

• Beneficiaries are identified by States/UTs and uploaded to the PM-KISAN Portal.
.        Essential details: State, District, Sub- District/Town, Block/Town, Village/Ward (all fields wherever Farmers land is present), Aadhaar, Farmer's Name, Farmer's Fathers/Husband's Name, Gender, Category, Date of Birth, Mobile Number, Spouse or Parent Details wherever applicable, etc

•        Land details: Khasra (Survey No.), Khata No. (Land Ownership ID), Land Area, Single/Joint Ownership Status, Mutation Date, Mutation Type, FRA Patta Holder Status, etc.
- Aadhaar is mandatory for registration and benefits transfer under the PM-KISAN scheme

The amount due to the beneficiaries under the scheme is to be paid directly into their Aadhaar seeded bank accounts through the mechanism of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). The amount will flow to the accounts of the beneficiaries held in destination banks, through the accredited bank of DA&FW and sponsoring banks of the States /UTs, using PFMS portal. The destination bank can be a Schedule Bank, Post office, Rural Bank, Cooperative Bank or any other Financial Institution as permitted by RBI and PFMS.

## Scheme Eligibility
Eligibility:
•        A farmer's family which includes husband, wife, and minor children who own cultivable land as per land records of the concerned State/UT. Only one member per family is eligible for the scheme.
•        Eligibility is based on land ownership records as of 01.02.2019.
•        Only succession/inheritance cases due to death of the previous owner after this date are considered for continued eligibility. Purchasers or transferees of land after 01.02.2019 (except by inheritance) are not eligible.
Exclusions:
•        Institutional landholders.
•        Families of current/former MPs/MLAs/Ministers, Mayors, District Panchayat Chairpersons, Constitutional Post Holders except former and present Gram Pradhan of Gram Panchayat
•        All serving/retired government officers & employees (except Class IV/Group D/MTS).
•        Pensioners with 110,000 monthly pension (except Class IV/Group COATS).
•        Income tax payees who have income tax liability at least for three years in the last five years and at least two years out to the three should be consecutive.
•        Professionals (Doctors, Engineers, Lawyers, CAs, Architects) engaged in practice.
•        NRIs as per Income Tax Act, 1961

Mandatory requirements under the PM-KISAN scheme:
1. Land Seeding on the PM-KISAN portal 
2.Aadhaar linked active bank accounts for Aadhaar based DBT payment
3. e-KYC under the PM-KISAN scheme

Land seeding is exempted for 14 States/UTs (Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, Puducherry, Delhi and Ladakh) given the status of land records in those States/UTs.

Land seeding is also exempted under the Vibrant Villages Programme. Vibrant Villages Programme is a centrally sponsored scheme launched in 2023 for the comprehensive development of the selected 662 villages in 46 blocks of the 19 districts in the States/UTs of Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, and Ladakh. The aim is to bring the development of villages of blocks on the northern border and improve the quality of life of individuals staying in identified border villages. Under these campaigns have been undertaken to identify, cover and saturate the PM Kisan scheme in these villages.

Land seeding and e-KYC is exempted for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups. Various campaigns have been initiated for PVTGs who are the most vulnerable sections of our society, to identify and cover all farmers from the PVTG community into the PM KISAN Scheme.

## Scheme Support
There is a stratified review monitoring mechanism at National, State and District Level. At the National level, the Review Committee will be headed by Cabinet Secretary. The States shall  notify the State and District Level Review Monitoring Committee. 
The States shall also notify State and District Level Grievance Redressal Monitoring Committees for looking into all the grievances related to implementation of the scheme. Any grievances or complaints which are received should be disposed of on merit preferably within two weeks' time. 
The PM-KISAN scheme has established a robust grievance redressal mechanism to ensure timely resolution of farmers' queries and concerns. Farmers can raise grievances through four modes, namely: 
i. physical letters or emails, 
ii. the PM-KISAN portal, 
iii. the Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS), and 
iv. the Kisan-eMitra Chatbot, which provides 
real-time assistance. This multi-channel approach ensures accessibility, efficiency, and transparency in grievance resolution, thereby enhancing farmer satisfaction and trust in the scheme's implementation. 
The Government of India has developed 'Kisan e- Mitra' (a voice-based Al Chatbot), which enables farmers to raise queries and get them resolved in their own language in real-time. The chatbot eliminates technological and language barriers, ensuring seamless access to information for all farmers. The Kisan-eMitra is now available in 11 languages, i.e., English, Hindi, Odiya, Tamil, Bangla, Malayalam, Gujarati, Punjabi, Telugu, Kannada and Marathi

## Additional Information
The State/UT Governments are mandated to register, verify, and upload the details of eligible farmers including land records, linking of Aadhaar with their bank accounts and eKYC for successful transfer of the benefits. As there was

## Title

Schemes

## Scheme Introduction
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) was launched from Kharif 2016 with aim to support production in agriculture by providing an affordable crop insurance product to ensure comprehensive risk cover for crops of farmers against all nonpreventable natural risks from pre-sowing to post-harvest stage. The Scheme has completed 16 crop seasons and is being implemented across States/Union Territories (UTs).   Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY)” is a Central Sector Scheme that aims to:  • Providing financial support to farmers suffering crop loss/damage arising out of unforeseen events.  • Stabilizing the income of farmers to ensure their continuance in farming.  • Encouraging farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.  • Ensuring credit worthiness of the farmers, crop diversification and enhancing growth and competitiveness of agriculture sector besides protecting the farmers from production risks.  • Promoting innovation & research of insurance and allied products so-as-to offer expanded choice to the farmers and the State Governments/UT Administrations 

## Scheme Benefits
The scheme ensures comprehensive risk coverage and promotes digitization and transparency in operations:

1. Covers prevented sowing, standing crop losses (yield loss), mid-season adversity, post-harvest losses, and localized calamities.
2. Farmers pay a uniform premium: 2% (Kharif), 1.5% (Rabi), 5% (commercial/horticulture crops); balance premium is shared by the Government.
3. Benefits include Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) into farmers’ bank accounts and use of technology (e.g., satellites, remote sensing) for transparent assessments.
4. Implementation is through a single national IT platform: National Crop Insurance Portal (NCIP).

## Scheme Eligibility
3. Coverage of Farmers

3.1 All farmers including sharecroppers and tenant farmers growing the notified crops in
the notified areas are eligible for coverage. However, farmers should have insurable
interest on the insured crops and lands. Such farmers are required to submit
necessary documentary evidence of land records prevailing in the State (Records
of Right (RoR), Land Possession Certificate (LPC) etc.) and/or applicable contract/
agreement details/ other documents notified/ permitted by concerned State
Governments/UT Administrations pertaining to sharecroppers/tenant farmers and
the same should be defined by the respective States/UTs in the notification itself.
Tribal farmers and forest dwellers having cultivation in forest land under FRA are also allowed
to be insured under the scheme. The farmers cultivating community owned land especially
as is practiced in NER states are also allowed to be covered under the scheme with
certification from village head or revenue authorities. All such farmers are also required to
essentially submit Aadhaar Number and declaration about the crop sown/ crops
intended to be sown.


3.1.1 Farmers availing the Kisan Credit Card (KCC)/Crop Loan/Loanee Farmers

3.1.1.1 The scheme is optional for all farmers including farmers who have been sanctioned
short-term Seasonal Agricultural Operations (SAO) loans though Kisan Credit Card
(KCC) for the notified crops from defined Financial Institutions (hereinafter referred
to as Loanee farmers). Existing Loanee farmers who do not want to get covered

PMFBY, States/UTs may adopt following approaches:

3.2.1.1 Full Universalization: Complete farmer database would be fetched on the NCIP
through the pre-validated, Land Parcel, Crop & Farmers KYC database of the
concerned State/UT. Enrolment through any other channels will not be required
under full universal coverage. The States may consider for opting full

farmers under the scheme by subsidizing the farmer’s premium partially or
completely. State/UT may decide to deduct a token amount from the farmer’s
account during enrolment. Farmers will be enrolled through the traditional enrolment
channels under the scheme.

## Scheme Support
Under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), a multi-tiered and structured Grievance Redressal Mechanism (GRM) has been established to ensure that farmers’ grievances are addressed in a time-bound, transparent, and effective manner. The key details from the official guidelines are as follows:

1. Multi-Level Grievance Redressal Committees
A. Taluka/Tehsil and District-Level Officers
Each district must designate Taluka/Tehsil and District-level Grievance Redressal Officers, preferably officers from the Agriculture or Horticulture departments.

These officers will be the first point of contact for farmers, banks, and insurance companies.

Grievances must be acted upon within 7 days of receipt.

If not resolved or the farmer is dissatisfied, the matter can be escalated to the District Level Grievance Redressal Committee (DGRC).

B. District-Level Grievance Redressal Committee (DGRC)
Headed by the District Magistrate/Collector.

Members include representatives from:

Farmers

Lead District Manager (LDM)

NABARD’s District Development Manager (DDM)

Insurance Company

Departments such as Agriculture, Horticulture, Cooperative, Revenue, Agricultural Statistics.

Can invite experts from Universities, IMD, SRSAC, etc.

The DGRC examines appeals and must dispose of cases within 15 days by issuing a speaking order.

If the grievance is found inadmissible, reasons must be recorded in writing.

C. State-Level Grievance Redressal Committee (SGRC)
Headed by the Principal Secretary/Secretary of the Nodal Department.

Includes representatives from:

State-Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC)

NABARD (CGM)

Insurance Companies

State departments

May invite subject experts (Agriculture Universities, IMD, STSU/STAC, etc.)

Handles:

Unresolved cases from DGRC

Grievances involving more than ₹25 lakh or affecting multiple districts

Must resolve grievances within 15 days of receipt.

Decisions are binding on all parties.

States must publicize details (name, address, email, contact) of the GR officers.

2. Centralized Digital Support: Krishi Rakshak Portal & Helpline (KRPH)
A toll-free helpline and digital portal to register, track, and resolve farmer grievances.

Each grievance is assigned a unique Ticket ID, and farmers are informed via SMS or Chatbot.

Grievances may be submitted via:

Phone call

Mobile app

Chatbot

Social media

Email

Written letters or in-person at Agriculture/Insurance offices

Complaints are escalated automatically as per defined timelines and escalation matrices.

Resolution must happen within 15 days.

Grievances can be re-opened if the farmer is not satisfied with the resolution.

The platform is integrated with other systems like:

IRDAI’s Bima Bharosa

RBI grievance portals

CPGRAMS

## Title
Soil Health Card

## Agricultural Domain
Schemes

## Scope
Central

## Scheme ID
shc

## Scheme Introduction
It is a Government of India’s scheme promoted by the Department of  Agriculture & Co-operation under the Ministry of Agriculture.  It will be implemented through the Department of Agriculture of all the State and Union Territory Governments.  A SHC is meant to give each farmer soil nutrient status of his holding and advice him on the dosage of fertilizers and also the needed soil amendments, that he should apply to maintain soil health in the long run.  SHC is a printed report that a farmer will be handed over for each of his holdings.  It will contain the status of his soil with respect to 12 parameters, namely N,P,K (Macro-nutrients) ; S (Secondary- nutrient) ; Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, Bo (Micro - nutrients) ; and pH, EC, OC (Physical parameters).  Based on this, the SHC will also indicate fertilizer recommendations and soil amendment required for the farm.  A sum of Rs. 190 per soil sample is provided to State Governments. This covers the cost of collection of soil sample, its test, generation and distribution of soil health card to the farmer.  The total outlay of the scheme is Rs. 568.54 crore for a period of 3 years. The scheme has been rolled out in the field during the current year i.e, 2015-16.  The Soil Health Card is a special government initiative that gives every farmer a detailed report about the health and nutrient status of their soil. In simple terms, it tells you exactly how healthy your soil is and what fertilizers or amendments you need to use to get the best crop yield without wasting money on unnecessary inputs.  The card is prepared after a proper soil test, checking for twelve important things like nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulphur, iron, zinc, and so on, along with the soil's pH and organic content. Based on these results, the card clearly explains how much of each fertilizer your soil really needs and what you can do to improve the soil over time.  You get this card once every three years, and it helps you track any changes in soil quality, making sure you’re always farming with the right information. The whole process, including testing and issuing the card, is organized by the Department of Agriculture, and it's completely supported by the government to help you grow healthier crops and save money on fertilizers.

## Scheme Benefits
Soil Health Card is completely free for farmers. The entire process—from collecting your soil sample, testing it in the laboratory, and preparing your Soil Health Card with recommendations—is fully paid for by the government. You do not have to pay any fees at any stage.  The aim of the scheme is to help every farmer understand their soil better and use fertilizers in the most efficient way, without any extra burden of cost. Even if you request your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra for a soil test, there should be no charge for the card or the service. The card will contain an advisory based on the soil nutrient status of a farmer’s holding. It will show recommendations on dosage of different nutrients needed.  Further, it will advise the farmer on the fertilizers and their quantities he should apply, and also the soil amendments that he should undertake, so as to realize optimal yields.   It will be made available once in a cycle of 3 years, which will indicate the status of soil health of a farmer’s holding for that particular period. The SHC given in the next cycle of 3 years will be able to record the changes in the soil health for that subsequent period.  

## Scheme Eligibility
The soil sample will be tested as per the approved standards for all the agreed 12 parameters in the following way: i. At the STLs owned by the Department of Agriculture and by their own staff. ii. At the STLs owned by the Department of Agriculture but by the staff of the outsourced agency.  iii.  At the STLs owned by the outsourced agency and by their staff.  iv.  At ICAR Institutions including KVKs and SAUs. v. At the laboratories of the Science Colleges/Universities by the students under supervision of a Professor/ Scientist.  The State Government will refer 1% of all the samples in a year to a ‘Referral Laboratory’ to analyze and certify on the results of Primary Laboratory. The State Government will be supported to establish ‘Referral Laboratories as required.  As per grid pattern adopted by the Ministry, 253 lakh soil samples will be tested every three years to generate approximately 14 crore Soil Health Cards.  You are eligible to get a Soil Health Card if you are a farmer in India, no matter how big or small your landholding is. The scheme is open to all farmers across the country, and the goal is to make sure everyone gets proper advice on soil nutrition and fertilizer use, whether you have irrigated or rain-fed land.  The process works like this: soil samples are collected from your field by trained staff, either from the Department of Agriculture or an approved agency. Sometimes, the government also appoints authorized agencies or involves students from agricultural colleges and Krishi Vigyan Kendras to help with the collection. These people are specially trained to take soil samples in the correct way, using proper tools and following scientific methods.  You don’t have to collect the sample yourself or worry about how to do it. The staff will visit your field, usually after the main crops have been harvested, and they will collect soil from several spots in your land to make sure the test results are accurate. They also take care to label everything clearly so your results match your farm.  The samples are taken after harvesting the main crops, and then tested in accredited laboratories. After testing, a Soil Health Card is prepared for your land and given to you with clear recommendations.  You don’t need to worry about complicated paperwork—the government and local agriculture officers handle the collection and testing.

## Scheme Support
Central Government:   Additional Commissioner (INM),  Government of India, Ministry of Agriculture, DAC, Krishi Bhawan, New Delhi, Telefax – 011  - 23384280 , E - mail – dwivediv@nic.in  State Government: The concerned State Director of Agriculture/ District Agriculture Officer. One can visit  www.soilhealth.dac.gov.in  or  www.agricoop.nic.in  for information on Soil Health Card Scheme.   National Informatics Center (NIC) has developed a web portal (www.soilhealth.dac.gov.in) for generation of uniform soil health card and fertilizer recommendation, which has four modules: a) Registration of Soil Samples. b) Testing of Samples in Soil Testing laboratory. c)  Fertilizer recommendation based on Soil Test Crop Response (STCR) equations. d) MIS Reports. 

## Additional Information
It is a facility for testing the soil sample for 12 parameters as indicated in reply to question number 2.  This facility can be static or mobile or it can even be portable to be used in remote areas.  In case the Soil health card is under process or not yet ready- Your Soil Health Card is under process. Since your sample has already been submitted, I recommend contacting the soil testing center or the local agriculture officer to check the status where the sample has been submitted. They can confirm whether your test results are ready but not uploaded, or if any detail needs correction. 

## Scheme Application
To apply for a Soil Health Card, you actually don’t need to fill out any complicated forms or visit many offices. The process is mostly managed by the government through your local Department of Agriculture. Here’s how it works in a simple way: trained staff or authorized agencies regularly visit villages to collect soil samples from farmers’ fields, usually after the main crops are harvested. You can approach your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra and let them know you want your soil tested—they will guide you and arrange for your soil sample to be collected. Once your soil sample is collected from your field, it is sent to a government-approved lab for testing. After the soil is tested, your Soil Health Card will be prepared with tailored advice and recommendations and will be handed over to you—either directly or through your village agriculture office. If you have not been approached for soil testing, you can always contact your nearest agriculture department office, Krishi Vigyan Kendra, or your village agriculture extension officer and request them to include your field in the next soil testing cycle. The government covers the cost, so you don’t need to pay anything for getting your Soil Health Card. You generally don’t need to worry about heavy documentation for the Soil Health Card. Since the process is handled by government staff or authorized agencies, they usually identify farmers through local records, village lists, or by checking your land details directly in coordination with local officials.  If you are specifically requesting your field to be included for soil testing, it can be useful to have some basic identification handy, like your Aadhaar card or any government-issued ID, and details about your landholding such as the Khasra number, land ownership documents, or your farmer registration details if you have them. These help local agriculture officers match your soil sample with your farm records, but in many cases, even this is handled smoothly with their existing village records.  You don’t have to submit piles of forms or run around for paperwork—the main thing is to stay in touch with your village agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra, and let them know you want your soil tested. They’ll guide you on what, if anything, is needed in your area. Soil samples will be drawn in a grid of 2.5 ha in irrigated area and 10 ha in rain- fed area with the help of GPS tools and revenue maps.  The State Government will collect samples through the staff of their Department of Agriculture or through the staff of an outsourced agency. The State Government may also involve the students of local Agriculture / Science Colleges. When the government staff or authorized agency comes to collect soil for your Soil Health Card, they follow a specific method to make sure the sample truly represents your land. To prepare this composite sample, they don’t just pick soil from one spot. Instead, they collect soil from five different places within your field—usually the four corners and the center. This soil is then mixed together thoroughly, and a portion is taken as the final sample for testing. This method ensures the test results reflect the actual condition of your entire plot, not just one small part. You don’t have to worry about counting or preparing the samples yourself. The trained staff or agriculture officers will handle all the technicalities for you. If you want to know exactly when or how the sampling will happen for your land, you can talk to your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra for more details.  Soil Samples are taken generally two times in a year, after harvesting of Rabi and Kharif Crop respectively or when there is no standing crop in the field.  Soil Samples will be collected by a trained person from a depth of 15-20 cm by cutting the soil in a “V” shape. It will be collected from four corners and the centre of the field and mixed thoroughly and a part of this picked up as a sample. Areas with shade will be avoided. The sample chosen will be bagged and coded.  It will then be transferred to soil test laboratory for analysis.

Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme implemented by the  Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) from the year 2015-16  to promote micro irrigation in the Country to benefit the farmer community. As a  part of the restructuring/rationalization of the schemes of DA&FW, PDMC Scheme  is being implemented under Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) from the year  2022-23.  The scheme is to be implemented through the mechanism of Direct Benefit  Transfer (DBT). Aadhaar details of the beneficiary are required to avail the  benefit of the programme. Aadhaar details need to be linked through a web  based registration process. States/UTs should ensure disbursement of subsidy in  a time bound manner.   The scheme will be monitored through web-portal of PDMC. Physical and  Financial progress achieved during the preceding month is required to be up loaded by states on the web-portal of PDMC.  The  Ministry is making efforts to bring two million ha area under micro irrigation per  year.   Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) focuses on enhancing water use efficiency  at farm level through Micro Irrigation viz. Drip and Sprinkler irrigation  systems.  Promote micro irrigation technologies in water intensive/consuming crops like  sugarcane, banana, cotton, paddy etc. and give adequate focus to extend coverage  of field crops under micro irrigation technologies.  Make potential use of micro irrigation systems for promoting fertigation. Promote micro irrigation technologies in water scarce, water stressed and critical  ground water blocks/districts   Link tube-well/river-lift irrigation projects with micro irrigation technologies for  best use of energy both for lifting and pressurized irrigation as far as possible.  Establish convergence and synergy with activities of on-going programmes and   schemes, particularly with created water source for its potential use, integration of  solar energy for pressurised irrigation etc.   Promote, develop and disseminate micro irrigation technology for agriculture and  horticulture development with modern scientific knowledge.   Support the initiatives of reuse of waste water in Agriculture/peri-urban  Horticulture through micro irrigation systems.   Create employment opportunities for skilled and unskilled persons, especially  unemployed youth for installation and maintenance of micro irrigation systems.  

## Scheme Benefits
The Automation unit  may be linked with solar energy wherever possible at the farm. It is desirable that  States should target 5% of Micro Irrigation coverage under the scheme with  Automation. The cost of automation may vary with the type of Automation adopted  by the beneficiary. For adoption of Automation in the Micro Irrigation system under  the scheme, the financial assistance to the beneficiary will be restricted on the  existing rate of subsidy to the indicative cost of Rs. 40000/ha.   States/UTs should prioritize implementation of MI through Cluster approach to  have effective integration of sources, connectivity, distribution and application.  The size of cluster may be 50 ha. & above in mainland states and 20 ha. in NE  & hilly states. Water User Associations/Groups, Farmer Producer Organizations,  Cooperative societies, Self-Help Groups, Growers’ Associations etc. shall be  encouraged to adopt Micro Irrigation in a cluster. In such cases the beneficiary  will be entitled to avail financial assistance through their respective  organizations / bodies. The total financial assistance available to the individual  beneficiary in the group would be 55% under the scheme. The land holding of  the beneficiary should be located in one contiguous area. Such farmers  groups/organizations may be allowed to avail an administrative/institutional  charges @ 3% of the cost of the Cluster.  

## Scheme Eligibility
The pattern of assistance payable to the beneficiary under the micro irrigation scheme will be 55% for small and marginal farmers and 45% for other farmers which will be met by both Central Government and State Government in the ratio of 60:40 for all states except the North Eastern and Himalayan States. In the case of these states, ratio of sharing is 90:10. For the Union Territories, funding pattern is 100% grant by the Central Government. The subsidy payable to the beneficiary will be limited to an overall ceiling of 5  hectare per beneficiary. Those beneficiaries, who have already availed subsidy  benefits for his /her farm, would be eligible for subsidy again for the same land  only after the end of projected life of the micro irrigation system which is 7 years.  The subsidy payment will be limited to the unit costs specified in the Operational  Guidelines of the scheme. 25% higher amounts will be taken into calculation of  subsidy for the North Eastern, Himalayan States and UTs of JK & Ladakh and  15% higher for States with low penetration of Micro Irrigation. The general framework of the Guidelines of the RKVY shall also be applicable for  PDMC.   Those beneficiaries, who have already availed subsidy benefits for his /her farm,  can not avail the assistance for the next seven years. A beneficiary if availed the  benefit of subsidy for micro irrigation for a particular farm would be eligible for  subsidy again for the same land only after the end of projected life of the micro  irrigation system which is seven years. However, the beneficiary may be allowed to  avail effective differential subsidy in case he intends to install Drip Irrigation  System on the same plot/field from the existing Sprinkler Irrigation System atleast  after three years to promote crop diversification irrespective of seven years  subsidy cycle.   Beneficiaries/Institutions that have opted for contract farming or taken land on  lease are also eligible for obtaining financial assistance under the scheme.  However, to become eligible, the beneficiary/institution shall have to produce lease  agreement for a minimum period of 7 years from the date of approval of  application by the MI implementing agency.  Fertilizer tank - to increase fertilizer use efficiency, fertilizer tanks have been  included in the list of equipment eligible for financial assistance. The  beneficiary can opt for either fertilizer tank or venturi system or automated  dosing system equipment and financial assistance will be provided for either  of those components.  

## Scheme Support

## Additional Information
The registration of manufacturers/companies under the scheme will be for a  period of 5 years. The registration will be open round the year. The registration  will, however, be subject to satisfactory performance by the company. In case of  violations, penalty provisions have been specified in the guidelines. Repeated  failures will lead to de-registration of the company with the approval of SLSC. Only BIS marked systems/components can be supplied under the scheme. The company will provide free service after sales to the beneficiary for a period of  at least three years from the date of installation of the system. If it fails to  provide free after sales service, action as appropriate similar to other consumer  products may be initiated.

## Title
ASHA FAQ

## Agricultural Domain
Schemes

## Scope
Central

## Scheme ID
pmasha

## Scheme Introduction
The Government of India launched Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (PM-AASHA) in September 2018 to provide remunerative price to the farmers of  pulses, oilseeds and copra in the event of the price falls below the notified Minimum Support Price (MSP). In September 2024, the Cabinet approved the continuation of the Integrated Scheme of PM-AASHA with Price Support Scheme (PSS), Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS) and Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) as its components during 15th Finance Commission upto 2025-26. The scheme has four components: 1) Price Support Scheme (PSS): Under this, Central Nodal Agencies such as NAFED and NCCF undertake procurement of pulses, oilseeds, and copra at MSP, in coordination with State Governments. 2) Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS) :  Under this, farmers are directly paid  the price difference between the  MSP and the selling/modal price of FAQ oilseeds selling in notified APMC markets through an transparent auction process.  The maximum coverage of price difference and quantity of oilseed will be up to 15% of MSP   (including 2% administrative cost) and  up to 40% of state  production respectively . States/UTs have an option to choose either PSS or PDPS for the particular oilseeds for that particular Season for the entire state.  If any State is willing to cover quantities beyond 40%, they may do so from their own resources. 3) Market Intervention Scheme (MIS):  MIS is implemented for procurement/coverage of of perishable agricultural and horticultural crops for which MSP is not announced to provide remunerative price to farmers.   4) Price Stabilization Scheme (PSF)- PSF is implemented to mitigate the hardships to consumers on account of price volatility in agri-horticulutral commodities. The objective of PSF scheme is to protect the consumers from extreme volatility in prices of agri-horticultural commodities and to make essential food commodities available at affordable prices. The PSF is implemented under the administration of Department of Consumer Affairs (DoCA) PSS, PDPS & MIS are implemented at the request of the State/UT Government. Together, these components create a flexible framework to protect farmers’ income and provide a fair return for their produce.

## Scheme Benefits
PM-AASHA provides a comprehensive framework to protect farmers from distress sale during peak arrival/harvesting  period of pulses, oilseeds and copra through timely market intervention which results in ensuring remunerative prices to farmers.   It safeguards farmers through direct procurement under PSS or paying price deficiency payments under PDPS.  While MIS ensures timely support for perishable and horticultural crops in case of price crashes. The scheme enhances income security, particularly for small and marginal farmers, by covering up to 40% of oilseed production under PDPS and extending procurement support through PSS. It also promotes crop diversification by incentivizing farmers to grow pulses and oilseeds, contributing to nutritional security and reducing import dependence. With flexibility for States to choose between PSS and PDPS, along with transparency through pre-registration, auction-based processes, and coordination with nodal agencies, PM-AASHA ensures benefits reach farmers directly. In sum, the scheme safeguards incomes, stabilizes markets, promotes diversification, and guarantees fair returns to farmers

## Scheme Eligibility
Eligible Crops Pulses, oilseeds, and copra are covered under Price Support Scheme (PSS). Oilseeds are covered under Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS). Horticultural and perishable crops are covered under Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) on request from States/UTs. Eligible Farmers All farmers producing the notified pulses, oilseeds and copra  are eligible to participate. Farmers must be pre-registered on the designated portal (through State Governments/Agencies) to avail benefits For PDPS, farmers must trade  prescribed Fair Average Quality (FAQ) oilseeds in the notified market yards to avail the  benefit of  deficiency payment. Procurement Conditions Procurement is allowed only for crops of Fair Average Quality (FAQ) as notified. Farmers must sell their produce in designated procurement centers/mandis within the stipulated procurement period. Under PDPS, payment is made directly to the bank accounts of farmers through DBT. Role of States/UTs States/UTs have the option to choose either PSS or PDPS for a particular oilseed in a given season/year. If States wish to cover quantities beyond the 40% limit, they must do so from their own resources.

## Scheme Support
State Nodal Departments/State  handle farmer queries, registration issues, and operational problems at the ground level. Central Nodal Agencies (NAFED, NCCF, etc.) address procurement- and payment-related issues. District-level committees monitor procurement operations and act as the first point of grievance redressal. Escalation mechanism: Unresolved cases are forwarded to the State Level Monitoring Committee and then to the Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), Government of India. Helplines & awareness camps are organized by States/UTs for farmer support.

## Additional Information
Under PM-AASHA, States/UTs play a critical role by conducting farmer awareness campaigns, facilitating registration through verification of land, crop, and bank details, and ensuring adherence to FAQ standards via quality control at procurement centres/markets. They must coordinate with Central Nodal Agencies (NAFED, NCCF etc.) and local APMCs for procurement, storage, and disposal. If a State chooses PDPS over PSS for a crop/season, the decision must be notified in advance to DA&FW to enable timely arrangements for auctions, price monitoring, and direct benefit transfers.

## Scheme Application
Farmer Registration Farmers intending to sell their produce under PSS or PDPS must pre-register on the designated portal (developed/maintained by the respective State Government or implementing agency). Registration requires details such as name, Aadhaar number, bank account (linked to Aadhaar), landholding details, crop sown, and expected production. Registration is generally done before harvesting, within the timelines notified by the State. Verification of Details The details furnished by farmers are verified by State Agriculture/Revenue authorities based on land records and crop-sown information. Only verified and approved farmers are eligible to participate in procurement or deficiency payment schemes. Sale of Produce Under PSS, registered farmers bring their produce of Fair Average Quality (FAQ) to the designated procurement centres/mandis during the procurement window. Procurement is carried out by Central Nodal Agencies (e.g., NAFED, NCCF) in coordination with State agencies. Under PDPS, farmers sell oilseeds in the notified markets through a transparent auction process within the stipulated period. Payment to Farmers For PSS, payment is made to farmers for the quantity procured at MSP directly into their bank accounts through DBT. For PDPS, the Central Government credits the price deficiency (difference between MSP and selling/modal price, subject to the prescribed limit) directly to pre-registered farmers’ bank accounts.

## Scheme Introduction
Agricultural machines take an important role to increase productivity with timely and precise fieldwork. To promote the usage of farm mechanization and increase the ratio of farm power to cultivable unit area up to 2.5 kW/ha, the scheme will be implemented in all the Indian states 
The SMAM scheme has both centrally sponsored and central sector scheme components. Objectives:
i) Increasing the reach of farm mechanization to small and marginal farmers
and to the regions where availability of farm power is low;
ii) Promoting Custom Hiring Services of agricultural machines to offset the
adverse economies of scale arising due to small landholding and high cost of
individual ownership;
iii) Creating awareness among stakeholders through demonstration, capacity
building activities and differentiated Information, Education and Communication strategies;
iv) Ensuring performance testing and certification at designated testing centers located all over the country;

## Scheme Introduction
Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme implemented by the  Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) from the year 2015-16  to promote micro irrigation in the Country to benefit the farmer community. As a  part of the restructuring/rationalization of the schemes of DA&FW, PDMC Scheme  is being implemented under Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) from the year  2022-23. The scheme is to be implemented through the mechanism of Direct Benefit  Transfer (DBT). Aadhaar details of the beneficiary are required to avail the  benefit of the programme. Aadhaar details need to be linked through a web  based registration process. States/UTs should ensure disbursement of subsidy in  a time bound manner. The scheme will be monitored through web-portal of PDMC. Physical and  Financial progress achieved during the preceding month is required to be up loaded by states on the web-portal of PDMC.  The  Ministry is making efforts to bring two million ha area under micro irrigation per  year. Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) focuses on enhancing water use efficiency  at farm level through Micro Irrigation viz. Drip and Sprinkler irrigation  systems. Promote micro irrigation technologies in water intensive/consuming crops like  sugarcane, banana, cotton, paddy etc. and give adequate focus to extend coverage  of field crops under micro irrigation technologies. Make potential use of micro irrigation systems for promoting fertigation. Promote micro irrigation technologies in water scarce, water stressed and critical  ground water blocks/districts. Link tube-well/river-lift irrigation projects with micro irrigation technologies for  best use of energy both for lifting and pressurized irrigation as far as possible. Establish convergence and synergy with activities of on-going programmes and  schemes, particularly with created water source for its potential use, integration of  solar energy for pressurised irrigation etc. Promote, develop and disseminate micro irrigation technology for agriculture and  horticulture development with modern scientific knowledge. Support the initiatives of reuse of waste water in Agriculture/peri-urban  Horticulture through micro irrigation systems. Create employment opportunities for skilled and unskilled persons, especially  unemployed youth for installation and maintenance of micro irrigation systems. Objectives of the Scheme •        Increase the area under Micro Irrigation technologies in agriculture to enhance water use efficiency. •        Increase productivity of crops and income of farmers through precision water management. •        Promote micro irrigation technologies in water intensive/consuming crops like sugarcane, banana, cotton, paddy etc. and give adequate focus to extend coverage of field crops under micro irrigation technologies. •        Make potential use of micro irrigation systems for promoting fertigation. •        Promote micro irrigation technologies in water scarce, water stressed and critical ground water blocks/districts. •        Link tube-well/river-lift irrigation projects with micro irrigation technologies for best use of energy both for lifting and pressurized irrigation as far as possible. •        Establish convergence and synergy with activities of on-going programmes and schemes, particularly with created water source for its potential use, integration of solar energy for pressurised irrigation etc. •        Promote, develop and disseminate micro irrigation technology for agriculture and horticulture development with modern scientific knowledge. •        Support the initiatives of reuse of waste water in Agriculture/peri-urban Horticulture through micro irrigation systems. •        Create employment opportunities for skilled and unskilled persons, especially unemployed youth for installation and maintenance of micro irrigation systems. •        Encourages solar pump integration with Micro Irrigation (MI).

## Scheme Benefits
•        Assistance/Subsidy up to 55% for small/marginal farmers and 45% of indicative cost for other farmers. •        Groups like FPOs, SHGs, Cooperatives can also apply under cluster approach under which uniform subsidy of 55% is applicable. •        The subsidy/assistance is shared in 60:40 (Centre:State) ratio For remaining states. •        For NE & Himalayan states, The subsidy/assistance is shared in ratio 90:10. •        For UTs, 100% central funding. •        Encourages solar pump integration with Micro Irrigation (MI). •        Only BIS-marked equipment/components allowed. •        Other Interventions viz. Water harvesting system for individuals, Construction of Tube wells / Bore wells (Shallow / Medium), Restoration / Renovation of small tank, Recharge of defunct bore well, Pipe/pre-cast distribution system, Water Lifting Devices (Electric, Diesel, wind / Solar), Petrol Irrigation Pumps- up to 15 hp to be provided as optional, if and only if a farmer opted to install micro-irrigation System in his/her field. The Automation unit  may be linked with solar energy wherever possible at the farm. It is desirable that  States should target 5% of Micro Irrigation coverage under the scheme with  Automation. The cost of automation may vary with the type of Automation adopted  by the beneficiary. For adoption of Automation in the Micro Irrigation system under  the scheme, the financial assistance to the beneficiary will be restricted on the  existing rate of subsidy to the indicative cost of Rs. 40000/ha. States/UTs should prioritize implementation of MI through Cluster approach to  have effective integration of sources, connectivity, distribution and application.  The size of cluster may be 50 ha. & above in mainland states and 20 ha. in NE  & hilly states. Water User Associations/Groups, Farmer Producer Organizations,  Cooperative societies, Self-Help Groups, Growers’ Associations etc. shall be  encouraged to adopt Micro Irrigation in a cluster.
